transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-07-21
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Mills (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Olivia Chen (Redwood SA), Priya Rao (Nova Lead ML Eng), Marcus Li (Nova Infra), Evan Brooks (Nova PM)

Summary:
High-level: deep technical review of prefix/prompt caching strategy across hosted, dedicated and on-prem deployments. Focus areas: cache key design for multi-tenant safety, hit-rate expectations on Nova prompt distribution, eviction and TTL strategies, quantization impacts on cache compatibility, and network/VPC considerations for prefix fetching in private deployments. Agreed next steps: share redacted prompts, run hit-rate sims, schedule pilot readiness call.

Topics: prefix key layout, tenant isolation, deterministic hashing, prefix expiry heuristics, cross-tenant collisions, serialization/versioning of cached KV, model variant compatibility (quantized vs fp16), local disk vs distributed cache, cache replication & SLOs, fallback policies.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sarah Mills: Alright everyone, thanks for joining. I'll do a 1-minute intro. I'm Sarah, AE at Redwood, with Daniel our SE and Olivia on the integration side. Nova team, want quick intros?
[00:12] Priya Rao: Hi, I'm Priya, lead ML at Nova. Marcus infra, Evan PM. We're looking to reduce token costs on our chat assistant and speed up latency for the high-value flows.
[00:22] Marcus Li: Hey all. Also worried about multi-tenant data isolation — we run multiple internal teams and some partner tenants.
[00:30] Daniel Park: Cool, great context. Today we'll focus on prefix caching: how we pick keys, how to keep tenants safe, and what happens when you run quantized variants.
[00:40] Evan Brooks: Quick ask: we have both cloud-hosted and an on-prem VM cluster for sensitive clients. How portable are Redwood caching strategies there?
[00:50] Olivia Chen: We'll cover that. There are some gotchas with network latency on VPC, and with disk-backed caches on-prem.

[02:10] Daniel Park: Let's start with how Nova is using prompts today. Priya, can you describe typical prompt patterns and the ratio of static prefix to dynamic user content?
[02:18] Priya Rao: Sure—rough numbers: about 35% of tokens are system and persona prefixes, 50% user content, rest is completions. But the sticky part is the prefix is long and often templated with per-tenant variations, so there's a lot of near-duplicates.
[02:34] Sarah Mills: Near-duplicates are prime for prefix caching if keys are designed to normalize tenant-specific values. Do you currently canonicalize things like user IDs or timestamps inside templates?
[02:45] Priya Rao: We try to strip timestamps, but IDs often remain. We're wary of canonicalizing too much because we need to preserve tenant-specific behavior.
[02:55] Daniel Park: Right. For multi-tenant safety, we recommend a layered key: include tenant-id as a separate namespace component, plus a normalized prompt fingerprint for the rest. So key = tenant||model-version||fingerprint. That avoids cross-tenant reuse while allowing intra-tenant hits on near-duplicates.
[03:12] Marcus Li: If we namespace with tenant, won't that reduce global hit rate? We have many low-traffic tenants.
[03:20] Daniel Park: It will reduce cross-tenant reuse, yes. There's a tradeoff: security/isolation vs aggregate hit rate. For Nova's case, given partner isolation requirements, we suggested strict namespacing but also a secondary shared fingerprint bucket for sanitized prompts where tenants opt-in.
[03:36] Evan Brooks: Can you explain the sanitized shared bucket pattern?
[03:40] Daniel Park: Sure — sanitize PII and tenant traces, then produce a second key without tenant id. Use that for non-sensitive prompts to get global hits. We mark these as lower-privilege caches. If a tenant hasn't opted in, we don't put their entries there.
[03:54] Priya Rao: That helps. One concern: how do we prove the sanitized variant doesn't change model behavior? Sometimes even small token changes shift completions.
[04:05] Daniel Park: Good point. We'll recommend A/B testing with a small percent rollout and evaluate regression metrics. Redwood's Optimize can track ngram divergence and hallucination rates for sanitized keys.

[06:10] Sarah Mills: Let's talk fingerprinting method. We usually use a stable canonicalizer (normalize whitespace, mask known placeholders) then hash with SHA-256 and truncate to 128 bits. We keep a version tag in the key for future algorithm changes. That way you can rotate fingerprint logic without invalidating all caches instantly.
[06:30] Marcus Li: Version tag is important. How do you handle TTLs? Nova has some prefixes that are stable for months and some that change per user session.
[06:40] Daniel Park: We recommend multi-tier TTLs: sticky prefixes get long TTLs (days-weeks), session-specific prefixes get short TTLs (minutes-hours). Also use adaptive eviction based on hit-rate decay — if a prefix hasn't been hit in X days, deprioritize.
[06:55] Priya Rao: Can we get a config that sets TTL per prefix pattern?
[07:00] Olivia Chen: Yes, Redwood supports per-key metadata tags and TTL override rules in Dedicated and Private deployments. We'll show sample configs.

[08:20] Daniel Park: Now on hit-rate expectations. With Nova's 3-day sample, we estimate intra-tenant prefix hit rates around 18-25% with strict tenant namespacing. If you sanitize and use shared buckets for templated prompts, that could bump to 40-55% on some endpoints.
[08:40] Priya Rao: Where does that number come from? Can you run it against our real traces?
[08:44] Daniel Park: Yes, that's a projection. Next step is running our sim pipeline against your redacted traces which we asked for in the next steps. We'll provide a CSV and a visual showing hit-rate over time and token savings.

[10:20] Marcus Li: On the implementation side — is Redwood's KV cache in-memory only or hybrid disk? For on-prem we prefer disk-backed for persistence across restarts.
[10:30] Olivia Chen: In hosted mode we use a distributed in-memory KV with optional persistence; Dedicated can be configured with local SSD-backed caches; Private on-prem can use LRU disk-backed caches or integrate with your memcached/redis if you prefer. We'll share the config matrix.
[10:48] Daniel Park: Important note: eviction policies differ when you have limited RAM but large disk — latency profiles change. Disk hits add ms to token latency and can affect tail. We typically keep hot prefixes in RAM and colder ones on local SSD.
[11:05] Evan Brooks: What about replication across nodes? We have redundant inference nodes.
[11:10] Daniel Park: We replicate metadata but don't replicate full KV across all nodes by default. Instead we use consistent hashing to route requests to the node that owns the key; fallbacks are local misses with upstream fetch. For Dedicated clusters you can enable cross-node replication, but there's a write amplification and consistency cost.

[13:00] Priya Rao: Quantization — we're running int8 for cost reasons. Are cached KV entries compatible across quantized and fp16 variants?
[13:08] Daniel Park: Generally no. The KV cache layout is model-architecture and implementation specific. If you change quantization or model variant, the KV embeddings/keys won't be compatible. We recommend including model-variant fingerprint in the cache key (model-name||quant-version||kv-schema-v) to prevent invalid reuse.
[13:28] Marcus Li: So a change from int8->fp16 invalidates a lot of cache, correct?
[13:32] Daniel Park: Yes. That's why we suggest warmup strategies: graceful rollout, keep both variants running, and populate the new cache gradually by shadowing traffic. Also use a fallback policy to the slower but correct path when a key isn't found.

[15:45] Sarah Mills: Another risk is stale KV after prompt template change. We saw teams accidentally keep old KV for weeks. How do you detect regression from stale prefixes?
[15:56] Daniel Park: Monitoring — track per-key hit-rate, response divergence vs non-cached baseline, and have alerts on sudden shifts. Redwood's console supports per-prefix metrics and alerting thresholds. Also include a key version in telemetry so you can map bad outputs to key versions and roll back if needed.

[18:10] Evan Brooks: For on-prem VPC deployments, network roundtrip to a centralized cache could hurt latency. Any patterns to avoid that?
[18:18] Olivia Chen: Co-locate the cache with inference nodes (local SSD or local in-memory). If you must centralize, use a fast internal network and prefer local caching of hot prefixes. Also configure adaptive prefetch for known sequences to warm local cache ahead of time.
[18:35] Marcus Li: How does prefetch work? Is it safe for multi-tenant?
[18:40] Daniel Park: Prefetch observes sequence patterns and precomputes likely KV states for upcoming tokens. For safety, prefetch respects tenant namespaces and privacy rules — it won't prefetch content from tenants that aren't allowed or sanitized.

[21:00] Priya Rao: A practical ask: can you show an example key layout?
[21:05] Daniel Park: Example: redwood:tenant:tenant123:model-gptx-1:int8:kvv3:sha128(abbrev).ttl=3600. We also store meta tags like "sensitive:false" so the cache system enforces sharing policies.
[21:22] Priya Rao: That helps.

[23:40] Sarah Mills: Let's dig into collision risk. If two tenants accidentally normalize differently, could two distinct prompts map to same fingerprint?
[23:50] Daniel Park: Hash collisions at the 128-bit truncated SHA level are astronomically unlikely, but human canonicalization mistakes can cause accidental collisions — e.g., aggressive masking that removes semantic tokens. We'll provide a canonicalization test suite and sample QA rules.
[24:08] Evan Brooks: On observability, can we get examples of the dashboards and logs?
[24:14] Olivia Chen: We'll share a deck with screenshots. You'll see per-tenant hit-rate, per-key latency distribution, cache evictions, and a trace view linking the model output to the key fingerprint.

[27:30] Priya Rao: Security question — if a tenant opts into shared sanitized buckets, how do we prove that sanitized data can't be re-associated later?
[27:40] Daniel Park: We recommend a two-step process: 1) deterministic sanitization with a reversible audit-disabled pipeline (we keep transformation rules but not originals), and 2) a privacy review and differential privacy checks for particularly sensitive fields. For high assurance, use Private deployments where keys never leave your VPC.

[30:00] Marcus Li: Network and firewall checklist for Private — do you have a doc?
[30:05] Olivia Chen: Yes, we'll send a checklist (port ranges, internal DNS, routing, IAM policies). We'll include sample iptables rules and a test harness.

[33:10] Daniel Park: A couple of gotchas we've seen: 1) model-rollout causing version mismatches, 2) TTLs that are too long after prompt schema changes, 3) over-aggressive sanitization reducing predictive quality.
[33:28] Priya Rao: Can Redwood automate TTL tuning?
[33:32] Daniel Park: We have an adaptive TTL feature that can propose TTLs based on decay curves and hit-rate elasticity. You can accept or override.

[36:50] Evan Brooks: Recovery from a bad rollout: what's the fast path?
[36:55] Sarah Mills: Rollback the model-serving variant and mark the offending key-version as deprecated; purge selectively by key prefix. Redwood can run targeted invalidations in Dedicated and Private within minutes.

[40:00] Olivia Chen: For the on-prem pilot, you should expect the initial integration to take 2 weeks: network, IAM, and storage config, plus deploy a small Dedicated-like cluster for validation. After that, 1-2 weeks of hit-rate sim and warmup.

[44:10] Priya Rao: Any recommendations on how to structure tenant opt-in for shared sanitized cache?

[44:20] Daniel Park: Provide a checkbox in tenant settings with clear docs on how sanitization works and a small experiment: run sanitized keys in shadow mode and report divergence. If drift is low, encourage opt-in and provide potential cost share.

[49:00] Marcus Li: How do you handle audit logs for cache mutations? We need to be able to show who populated or invalidated a key for SOC2.
[49:10] Olivia Chen: Redwood logs cache write/evict operations with key fingerprints and operation metadata. In Private deployments logs can be shipped to your SIEM; in Hosted we provide an export.

[52:50] Sarah Mills: Ok, let's do a quick recap and next steps. Daniel, can you summarize technical asks?
[52:58] Daniel Park: Sure—(1) run hit-rate sim on redacted traces and return CSV and visuals, (2) propose key/fingerprint versioning and example TTL policies, (3) share VPC/on-prem checklist and prefetch config samples.
[53:12] Priya Rao: We'll upload redacted traces by Friday, and I'll loop in security for the sanitized bucket review.
[53:20] Evan Brooks: We'll plan the on-prem pilot starting mid-August.

[55:00] Sarah Mills: Great. I'll circulate meeting notes and the artifacts Olivia mentioned. Any final Qs?
[55:10] Marcus Li: One small thing — are there any licensing limits on storing cache entries for partners?
[55:16] Sarah Mills: Not beyond contract; we'll put specifics in the pilot SOW.
[55:25] Priya Rao: Thanks everyone.
[55:28] Daniel Park: Thanks, bye.
[55:30] [call ends]
